name: PT Putra Mandiri Jembar Tbk

frontmatter.title: Putra Mandiri Jembar: a Mitsubishi dealer carrying a government truck contract
frontmatter.summary: Initiation on the Mitsubishi, Nissan and Mercedes-Benz dealer that won the Red and White Cooperatives truck contract. We rate the shares BUY with a Rp187 target against a Rp137 price: the market discounts a sharper post-contract revenue cliff than we forecast, the balance sheet carries net cash and the shares trade below book. The thesis fails on delivery pace, single-franchise concentration and a free float too small for most mandates.
thesis: The cooperative truck contract re-bases the revenue line for two years without creating a moat: the founding family controls the company, Mitsubishi Corporation holds a blocking stake, and the public float is under a tenth [S7][F31].

First-half results show the operating leverage working: revenue up by more than half and net profit up by more than one and a half times, with the after-sales annuity on the delivered trucks still ahead [S9].
The balance sheet is the floor under the valuation: net cash, no bonds, property carried at revaluation, and the shares trade at a discount to book on our forecast [S5].

The binding constraint is access rather than value: a public float near a tenth and turnover of a few hundred million rupiah a day earn a liquidity haircut large enough to absorb most of the upside [S0].

catalysts.event: Third-quarter LK, the first reporting period that covers a full quarter of truck deliveries
Monthly Gaikindo wholesale data to the year end, the cleanest read on whether the dealer market recovery holds
First anniversary of the contract start, with disclosure on delivered units and any follow-on tranche
Full-year results and the FY2026 dividend declaration at the stated payout policy

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Putra Mandiri Jembar with an BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp187 against a last price of Rp137, a total return of 44.2% including the dividend we expect over the next twelve months. Put simply, we think the market is treating a genuine two-year earnings step-change as if it were an accounting artefact, and we think it is doing so for a defensible reason and to an indefensible degree. The company is a Mitsubishi franchise dealer group that also holds one Mercedes-Benz and one Nissan outlet, and in April 2026 it became the vehicle supplier to the Red and White Cooperatives programme through its principal distributor [S2][S7].

The share price sits at 0.6x book value and 5.4x our FY2026E earnings, with a 7.4% dividend yield on the payout policy the board has actually followed [S0][S5]. The company holds net cash, has no bonds outstanding, and funds its inventory from supplier credit and customer prepayments rather than borrowings [S5][F9]. That combination — a profitable, net-cash, dividend-paying dealer at two thirds of book — usually signals either a governance discount or a peak-earnings fear. Here it is both, plus a float so small that the stock cannot absorb institutional money without moving.

Our valuation is a probability-weighted blend of a discounted cash flow, an enterprise-value-to-EBITDA cross-check and a price-to-earnings cross-check, and then a liquidity discount because turnover is well below the threshold at which the house will treat a name as investable at full value. The discounted cash flow alone produces Rp198 a share, worth just over half the weight; the trailing multiple cross-checks produce Rp172 and Rp84 and sit below it, for reasons we set out in the valuation section rather than dismiss [S0].

The most likely path, in our view, is that FY2026 revenue lands a little below the company's own target because the second half has to run at close to twice the first half to get there, and that the truck contract then tails off through FY2027 and FY2028 before the base dealer business resumes growing with the national market [F24][F17][S8]. On that path the shares are worth more than they cost. The reverse calculation says the current price discounts a steeper post-contract decline than we forecast, which is the variant view: we are paid for believing deliveries happen, not for believing the programme is permanent.

Franchised car dealerships are a working-capital business dressed as a retail business. The manufacturer sets the wholesale price, allocates the models, owns the brand and can move a territory; the dealer earns a thin margin on the metal and a fat margin on the service bay, the parts counter and the trade-in. That is why dealer groups the world over trade at low multiples of book and why their earnings collapse faster than their revenue when volumes fall, because the fixed cost of the showroom does not move with the cycle.

PT Putra Mandiri Jembar is a holding company for a group of automotive businesses built around the Mitsubishi franchise in Indonesia. The operating dealer is PT Dipo Internasional Pahala Otomotif, which the company describes as the continuation of a Mitsubishi dealership relationship that reaches back decades, and which is the entity that signs the manufacturer-side contracts [S2][S4]. The group also runs a Nissan and Datsun outlet appointed in 2019, a single Mercedes-Benz outlet, a corporate vehicle rental business, a used-car trading subsidiary, an e-commerce parts portal and a spare-parts trading joint venture formed with Mitsubishi Corporation [S2][S4].

The physical footprint is 65 Mitsubishi showrooms plus the single Mercedes-Benz and the single Nissan and Datsun outlets, spread across 49 cities and 14 provinces in Sumatra, Jakarta, Java and Kalimantan [S2][F28][F29][F30]. This is a regional rather than national network: it is concentrated in the western and central islands where the family's dealerships were built, and it does not cover Sulawesi, eastern Indonesia or Bali. For the avoidance of doubt on a point that circulates in the market, the group holds no Daihatsu or Suzuki franchise; it is a Mitsubishi business with two small non-Mitsubishi outlets [S2][S7].

Revenue is overwhelmingly metal. In FY2025 vehicle sales were IDR9,301.0bn of IDR10,328.9bn of net sales, with spare parts at IDR521.5bn, service at IDR220.4bn, and smaller lines for body repair, rental and other revenue [S5][F4][F5][F6]. The profit pool is the mirror image. Vehicle cost of sales of IDR9,135.8bn leaves a gross margin near two per cent, while service cost of sales of IDR73.9bn against service revenue leaves a gross margin above sixty per cent, and spare parts earn a mid-teens margin [F7][F8]. After-sales is therefore a small slice of revenue and roughly a third of gross profit, which is the structural reason a dealer fights to keep the car in its own service bay after the warranty ends.

The group employed 2,614 people at the end of FY2025, the great majority of them in the Mitsubishi dealer subsidiary [S4][F38]. Strategy as disclosed is not complicated: grow the fleet segment, renovate and add outlets, push after-sales penetration and use information systems to shorten the sales cycle [S4]. The stated focus on fleet is what made the cooperative contract a natural extension rather than a departure, because fleet sales are won on price, specification and the ability to deliver volume, not on showroom location.

The contract itself is the single most important fact about the company today. Through DIPO, acting as an authorised dealer appointed by PT Krama Yudha Tiga Berlian Motors under a master contract, the group will supply 20,600 six-wheel trucks to PT Agrinas Pangan Nusantara for the government's Red and White Cooperatives programme, in a procurement worth IDR10,840.0bn at contract value, effective from early April 2026 after a bank guarantee and an upfront payment of IDR2,840.0bn from the buyer [S7][F14][F15][F16]. The scope is not only delivery: the contract also obliges DIPO to provide after-sales support to the cooperative operator, which is the part of the deal that could outlast the metal [S7].

Control sits with the founding family. PT Pahalamas Sejahtera holds a little over half the shares, Suhanti Poniman holds a further slice, and Mitsubishi Corporation holds exactly a third, leaving a public float just under a tenth [F31][F32][S4]. The Mitsubishi Corporation stake is the single most reassuring fact in the governance section: a trading house that understands this industry better than any domestic investor has chosen to hold a blocking stake through the cycle rather than sell into it.

A franchise dealer group is really a portfolio of local monopolies with expiry dates. Each outlet has a territory, a brand and a service catchment, and each of those can be renegotiated or reassigned. The value of the group is therefore the sum of the cash the territories throw off before the manufacturer decides to redraw the map, which is why dealer businesses are valued on cash flow over a defined horizon rather than on a growth perpetuity.

The Indonesian passenger and commercial vehicle market is small, cyclical and Japanese-dominated. National wholesales were 803,687 units in 2025, a contraction on the prior year, while retail sales ran ahead of wholesale as dealers worked down stock [S4][F34]. The recovery since then has been violent: wholesales over the ten months to October 2026 reached 760,476 units against 561,405 in the comparable period of 2025, an increase of more than a third, with October alone running above eighty thousand units and ahead of the prior month [S8][F35][F36]. Retail sales rose by less than wholesale, which tells you the recovery is being pushed through the factory-to-dealer channel rather than pulled by consumers [S8].

For a dealer group the relevant question is not the size of the market but the share of it that flows through its own showrooms. PMJS does not disclose a market share, and we would not trust a derived one, because its revenue includes fleet transactions that are lumpy and, in FY2026, dominated by a single government programme [S4][S7]. What we can say is that the base dealer business tracked the market: FY2025 revenue rose while national wholesales fell, and the first quarter of FY2026, before any truck revenue, grew at close to the market rate [S10][F34]. That suggests a network holding share rather than losing it, which is the minimum a franchise dealer must do.

The demand driver that matters for the next two years is the cooperative programme. Agrinas Pangan Nusantara has announced plans to procure up to 160,000 vehicles for the cooperatives programme nationally, of which the PMJS tranche is a fraction [S7][F39]. That larger number is the bull case and the risk at the same time: it is an intention, not a contract, and the first tranche went to one dealer because that dealer could deliver against a Mitsubishi master contract, not because a competitive tender allocated territory fairly. Whether a second tranche follows, and to whom, is a policy decision we cannot forecast and do not assume.

Competitive position is weak in the structural sense and adequate in the commercial sense. The five forces are unkind: supplier power is close to absolute, because the group's revenue depends on a single distributor relationship with Krama Yudha Tiga Berlian Motors and, behind it, Mitsubishi Motors; buyer power has risen sharply now that the largest customer is a state-owned procurement entity that dictates specification and payment terms; rivalry among Mitsubishi dealers in the same cities is on price; new entrants arrive through Chinese brands appointing fresh dealer networks; and the substitute for a new Mitsubishi is a used one, which the group also sells through its used-car subsidiary [S2][S7][S10].

The moat, such as it is, has three strands. The first is the franchise territory itself, which is contractual rather than proprietary and can be reallocated. The second is the installed base: every car sold generates service, parts and body-repair revenue for a decade, and the group's after-sales gross margin is the evidence [F8]. The third is land. The properties are carried on a revaluation model, which means the balance sheet reflects something closer to market value than historic cost, and a dealer that owns its sites has a cost advantage over one that rents [S5]. None of these strands is strong enough to justify a premium multiple; together they justify not valuing the business at nothing, which is roughly what the current enterprise value does.

The installed-base annuity is the most durable value in the deal and the hardest to size, which is why it sits in the bull case rather than the base. Service revenue was IDR220.4bn in FY2025 at a gross margin above sixty per cent, and spare parts IDR521.5bn at a mid-teens margin, together roughly a third of gross profit [F5][F6][F8][S5]. The contract adds 20,600 trucks to that base, but the company discloses neither units in service nor a retention rate, so we do not put a per-truck annuity into the base case: we carry the existing run-rate and treat incremental service and parts on the delivered fleet as bull-case upside [S7].

External influences are mostly macro. The rupiah is the channel through which imported vehicle content and consumer credit costs reach the dealer, and the house macro deck (fund record the November 2026 vintage) has the currency at 18,103 against the dollar with a forecast of 18,350 for FY2027E, a depreciation path consistent with the balance-of-payments pressure regime the house is carrying. The policy rate is at 5.8% and inflation at 3.3%, a combination that keeps the cost of financing a car high relative to household income and keeps the recovery dependent on fleet and institutional demand rather than on consumers [S4].

Regulation touches the group in two places. Vehicle type approval, emissions and tax treatment are set nationally and are the same for every dealer, so they do not differentiate. The cooperative programme is itself a policy instrument, which means its pace, its specification and its continuation are political variables rather than commercial ones, and we treat them that way in the scenarios [S7].

Indonesia's car market has never sustained the volumes its population implies, because household credit penetration is low, down-payment requirements are high and the used market absorbs buyers who cannot finance new. That is why wholesales oscillate around a million units rather than growing smoothly, and why a dealer group's earnings are levered to a cycle it cannot influence. The franchise system also means the manufacturer, not the dealer, captures most of the value of a recovery, through wholesale pricing and allocation.

The historical record is a business going sideways into a trough and then jumping. Revenue was IDR11,509.5bn in FY2022, IDR10,494.2bn in FY2023, IDR9,646.0bn in FY2024 and IDR10,328.9bn in FY2025, so the group lost ground for two years and recovered a little of it in the third [S5]. Gross profit fell from IDR832.1bn to IDR661.8bn over the same span, a gross margin compression from the low sevens to the mid sixes, and operating profit fell from IDR421.6bn to IDR189.9bn [S5]. That is the shape of a dealer with a fixed cost base and a shrinking volume: the margin does not collapse, the operating line does.

We restate four historical lines from the audited statements, because the data pack is wrong on all four. Operating cost is the largest. On the audited definition — selling and marketing plus general and administrative less other income — operating cost was IDR471.8bn in FY2025 and IDR429.4bn in FY2024, against the larger pack figure, which fails to net the other-income credit off the expense lines; restating cost alone would move nothing, so we also take operating profit from the same statement, IDR189.9bn in FY2025 and IDR171.8bn in FY2024, and the two restatements are consistent by construction: gross profit less the restated operating cost equals the restated operating profit [F55][F56][F57][F58][S5]. Depreciation charged to profit or loss was IDR65.8bn in FY2025 and IDR57.5bn in FY2024, against the materially larger figure the data pack carries, which appears to capture the movement in gross block rather than the charge that actually ran through the income statement [F1][F2][S5]. Financial expenses were IDR9.7bn in FY2025 rather than the lower figure in the pack, because the audited line includes interest on lease liabilities [F3][S5]. The EBITDA base from which the multiples are struck is now struck on the audited statements, and it agrees line for line with the EV/EBITDA cross-check: IDR255.7bn in FY2025.
:::table:fin_summary :::

The FY2025 profit was flattered by items that did not repeat in the same proportion. Other income of IDR62.7bn was roughly a third of pre-tax profit, and of that IDR47.6bn was manufacturer subsidy for sales, discount and promotion and IDR11.3bn was dealer incentive [F10][F11][F12][S5]. Those are real cash items and they are part of the economics of a Mitsubishi dealer, but they are also the first thing a manufacturer trims when it wants to take margin back. In the first quarter of FY2026 other income fell to IDR13.2bn, against a much larger figure a year earlier, which is direct evidence that the subsidy line is discretionary and that the FY2026 profit growth is coming from volume and mix rather than from support payments [S10][F44].

The cash flow needs to be read carefully, because the headline number is not earnings, and because it came from two balance-sheet lines rather than one. Cash generated from operations was close to ten times net profit in FY2025: customer advances and unearned revenue rose from a little over a tenth of a trillion rupiah to IDR1,322.8bn, and trade payables to third parties rose from IDR1,028.6bn to IDR2,226.1bn, more than doubling [S5][F9][F47][F48]. Inventory rose from IDR1,048.1bn to IDR1,914.6bn and trade receivables fell from IDR645.3bn to IDR532.8bn, so the working-capital swing was roughly half supplier credit and half customer prepayment, partly consumed by the stock build [S5][F46][F49][F50][F51]. The advances are the prepayment mechanism for fleet and cooperative orders, and the inventory build is consistent with trucks awaiting delivery rather than unsold cars; the payables extension is supplier credit that reverses when terms normalise, and we treat that reversal as a risk in the bear case.

The latest actual already shows the normalisation. In the first half of 2026 operating cash flow was IDR191.2bn against net profit of IDR127.2bn, a cash conversion of about one and a half times rather than ten, and IDR284.0bn of the cash balance sits in a restricted placement [F40][F18][F52][S9]. The FY2025 ratio was a working-capital event, not a permanent feature of the business: it is why we carry a working-capital ratio of -4.5% of revenue, consistent with the ratio at 30 June 2026, rather than capitalising the 2025 cash conversion into the terminal value [S0][S9].

Our forecast is built bottom-up from those two facts: a contract that has to be delivered, and a base dealer business that grows with a market which is already up by more than a third [S7][S8]. Revenue reaches IDR18,282.1bn in FY2026E, which is the company's own target of IDR18,900.3bn less a small haircut for delivery pace, then IDR17,550.8bn, IDR15,304.3bn, IDR15,947.1bn and IDR16,585.0bn as the contract runs off and the base business takes over [F24][S8]. The haircut is not caution for its own sake: management delivered about ninety-four per cent of its FY2025 revenue target and the same proportion of its profit target, and the first half produced IDR6,110.0bn of revenue, so the target requires a second half close to twice the first against a historical second-half skew of about one and two thirds [F26][F27][F17][S0].

Margins follow the mix. Gross margin is 7.3% in FY2026E, which is the first-quarter actual: the only 2026 gross-profit line in an archived document is the first quarter, before truck deliveries, at IDR2,442.0bn of gross profit on IDR177.8bn of revenue [F21][F23][S10]. No archived source carries a second-quarter gross-profit line, so we do not claim to have measured fleet dilution during the delivery phase; we carry the audited-quarter rate and let the fade carry the risk instead, to 6.7% by FY2028E and 6.6% in the terminal year, back to the FY2025 level as the contract leaves the mix [S5][S7].

The definition of operating cost matters as much as its level. On the consistent basis — selling and administrative expense net of manufacturer subsidy and other income — the ratio is 4.2% of revenue in FY2026E, below the FY2025 ratio of about four and a half per cent because fleet volume dilutes a fixed base [S5]. The Q1 press report's "total operating expenses" figure includes net finance and final tax; stripped back to SG&A net of other income the first-quarter ratio is a little over five per cent, and the half-year bridge from the archived pre-tax profit of IDR196.8bn, at the first-quarter gross margin, puts the half-year ratio near three and a half per cent [S10][S9][F19]. The forecast ratio rises to 4.7% once the contract is gone and the dealer business has to carry the cost base alone [S5].

The result is an operating margin of just over three per cent in FY2026E, falling to about two per cent by FY2028E, which is not a heroic assumption for a dealer and is roughly where the business was in FY2025 before the contract [S5]. Net profit attributable to owners reaches IDR349.1bn in FY2026E, or Rp25 a share, and total net profit is IDR431.0bn. The company's IDR309.0bn profit target is stated on a total-profit basis, as its own FY2025 precedent shows: it set a IDR156.2bn target against a total net profit of IDR146.1bn, the ninety-four per cent delivery the annual report cites [F27][S4]. On that same total basis our forecast is about a third above the plan, and the premium is a considered difference of view rather than a slip in basis. The plan implies a parent net margin below the 1.9% we forecast, while the first half alone earned IDR196.8bn of pre-tax profit against IDR198.4bn for the whole of FY2025, and the second half carries roughly twice the first half's revenue [F17][F19][S9]. Our full-year pre-tax margin is below the first-half rate, so we are not extrapolating the best quarter: we are declining to assume that a plan published with the FY2025 accounts already captures a contract that only became effective in April [S7].

Capex is the one line where the market's habit of extrapolating the FY2024 land-buying year would mislead. Capital expenditure was IDR163.6bn in FY2025 and IDR75.8bn in the first half of FY2026, which annualises to about one and a fifth per cent of revenue [F20][S9]. We hold 1.2% of revenue, enough to renew the asset base and fund the growth the terminal rate implies on a property book worth roughly a fifth of revenue, and well below the FY2024 spike [S5]. Working capital is negative and stays negative: the ratio is -4.5% of revenue while the contract runs, and eases to -3.8% as the prepayment float unwinds [S5][F9].

The balance sheet is the least complicated part of the story. Cash and equivalents were IDR1,860.0bn at the end of the first half against debt of IDR117.3bn, and equity was IDR3,380.0bn including minorities [S9][F41][F43][S5]. There are no bonds, no medium-term notes and no material related-party borrowing beyond a shareholder loan of IDR23.9bn at a commercial rate [F13][S5]. On our forecast the group stays in net cash through the horizon, which is unusual for a dealer and is a direct consequence of being paid in advance by its largest customer.

Earnings quality flags are mixed rather than alarming, and the direction has changed. The FY2025 accruals ratio was strongly negative because cash from operations dwarfed net profit, but the cause was the combined advance and payables inflow rather than conservative accounting, and an analyst who took that cash flow at face value would overstate the sustainable earning power of the business [F9][F47][F48][S5]. The first half of 2026 shows the normalisation: operating cash flow of IDR191.2bn on net profit of IDR127.2bn, about one and a half times, with a restricted-cash placement of IDR284.0bn [F40][F18][F52][S9]. Inventory grew faster than cost of sales, which the contract explains and which would be a red flag in a normal year [F46][F49]. Receivables fell and remain modest relative to revenue, so the group is not lending to its dealers or its customers [F50][F51]. The payables extension is the flag we watch: a supplier that pulls terms back would reverse the 2025 funding benefit at the same time as the advance unwinds. We could not reach the exchange notation page from this environment, so we cannot confirm the trading board; the data pack carries no special notation flag, and we treat that as unverified rather than clean [S0].

Direct-method cash flow statements, which Indonesian issuers use, do not show a depreciation add-back. The consequence is that a data provider scraping the cash flow statement will often report a depreciation figure that is either missing or drawn from the wrong place, and an analyst who calibrates a cash cost off that number will be systematically wrong. Indonesian dealership accounts also book manufacturer support as other income rather than as a reduction of cost of sales, which inflates operating margin relative to the economics.

A dealer with a windfall, a negative working-capital cycle and a net cash balance sheet is best valued on free cash flow, because the earnings-based methods will either capitalise the windfall or ignore it. We therefore weight a discounted cash flow at just over half, an enterprise-value-to-EBITDA cross-check at nearly a third and a price-to-earnings cross-check at a seventh. The DCF is the only method priced on the forecast earnings base; the two multiples are struck on trailing earnings, so we give the one that corrects least for the cycle — the enterprise-value method, which uses EBITDA rather than trough net income — the larger of the two cross-check weights [S0]. The discounted cash flow runs ten explicit years so that the terminal value is struck after the contract has gone, not on the contract year.
:::table:wacc :::

The cost of capital is built from the macro deck rather than from a house view. The ten-year rupiah government yield is 7.4%, we strip the sovereign default spread of 1.6% so as not to double count country risk, add the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, and apply an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry configuration [S0]. With gearing of 5.4% the levered beta is 0.94, giving a cost of equity of 12.1% and, after a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and the statutory tax shield, a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9% [S5]. That sits inside the house band for rupiah names and reflects a business with almost no debt and a cyclical, low-moat operating profile.
:::table:dcf :::

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of IDR1,551.4bn and an equity value of Rp198 a share, with the terminal value carrying 50.9% of the total [S0]. The bridge from enterprise to equity value is where a net-cash dealer differs from a leveraged one: we add the cash, deduct the modest debt, deduct the minority interest that sits against the dealer subsidiary and add the small investment balance, which is why the equity value is well above the enterprise value [S5]. A reader who ignores the minority interest or who forgets that the cash belongs partly to the minorities will overstate the per-share value; we have tried not to.
:::table:valuation :::

The multiple cross-checks disagree with the primary method, and the disagreement is the most important thing in this section. The P/E method returns Rp84 at 9.8 times earnings, and the enterprise-value-to-EBITDA method returns Rp172 at 4.7 times [S0]. Both are struck on trailing FY2025 figures, which are the last year before the contract and therefore the worst base in the forecast window. Applied to a trough year they understate value by construction, and the P/E does so far more than the EBITDA method because parent earnings of Rp9 a share are the trough itself. That is why we have cut the P/E weight from the template's three tenths to a seventh: on FY2026E earnings of Rp25 the same multiple would produce a value well above the DCF, and a twelve-month target built on trough earnings would embed the pre-contract cycle rather than the most likely path [S0]. We keep the method as a downside cross-check rather than letting it disappear, and we say plainly that the discount to the primary method is a statement about the earnings base, not about the multiples, which are unremarkable for a dealer at this point in the cycle.

The DCF also has to pass the multiple-survival test, and it passes only partly. The terminal value implies an exit multiple of about five times EBITDA against an entry multiple just under three on our forecast, so roughly four fifths of the multiple expansion sits inside the terminal value [S0]. Terminal reinvestment runs at about two fifths of NOPAT at the 4.0% terminal growth rate, implying a return on incremental capital near one tenth, below the 11.9% weighted average cost of capital [S0]. That is the honest weakness: a franchised dealer does not earn excess returns in perpetuity, which is why we fade the contract windfall by FY2028, let the base business grow at the nominal market rate from FY2029 and keep the terminal share of value near half rather than the three quarters a genuine compounder would carry [S5]. Owner earnings bridge from reported net income through the D&A add-back, the working-capital ratio and capex of 1.2% of revenue; the full cash-flow build is in the DCF table [S0].

The probability-weighted value across the three scenarios is Rp234, and the liquidity discount takes it to Rp187. The discount is not a fudge: the public float is 9.0% of the shares, the controlling family and Mitsubishi Corporation together hold the rest, and three-month average daily turnover is 258,108,321 rupiah, which is far below the level at which the house will treat a position as exitable at full value [F32][S0]. A buyer who cannot sell is not buying the same asset as a buyer who can, and charging for that in one visible line is more honest than burying it in the discount rate.

The discount is also the one part of the valuation that a corporate action can change without any change in earnings. The house haircut is 20.0%; a secondary sale or placement that lifted daily turnover above the threshold would halve it and add roughly an eighth to the target, with no change in the cash flows. We do not put that in the base case because nothing is announced, but it is the cheapest upside in the name and the reason we treat float widening as a catalyst rather than a detail [S0].
:::table:sensitivity :::

The sensitivity is lopsided, which is the real risk in the name. A percentage point on the weighted average cost of capital moves the discounted value by roughly seven per cent, and a percentage point on terminal growth by about four per cent; a percentage point on the gross margin moves the twelve-month value by more than a third, and two points on revenue growth by about a tenth [S0]. In other words this is not a valuation that turns on the discount rate. It turns on whether the trucks are delivered at the margin we assume and whether the dealer business holds its pricing after the contract ends.

What the price implies is the cleanest statement of the variant view. Holding everything else at our assumptions, the current share price is consistent with FY2027E revenue falling by -9.9% rather than the -4.0% we forecast [S0]. That is a materially sharper post-contract cliff than our base case, and it is closer to our bear case than to our base. We are not arguing that the market is wrong to apply a liquidity discount or to distrust a government contract; we are arguing that it has applied both twice.

On our numbers the shares trade at 0.6x book, 5.4x FY2026E earnings and 0.5x FY2026E EBITDA, with a 7.4% dividend yield [S0]. The enterprise-value multiple is the smallest of the three and it is an artefact, not a bargain: enterprise value nets off the group's cash and customer advances, so the same forecast EBITDA bought through the market capitalisation costs several times more. Read the book and earnings multiples, which are struck on equity, as the informative ones. For a business earning a return on equity close to its cost of equity in the trough year and comfortably above it when the contract delivers, with net cash and a demonstrated payout, those are not demanding multiples. They are the multiples of a company the market expects to give the money back.

Reverse discounted cash flow is a discipline rather than a forecast. Instead of arguing about a target multiple, you solve for the operating assumption that makes the present value equal the price, and then ask whether that assumption is plausible. For a cyclical business the answer is usually that the market is extrapolating the last two years of the cycle in whichever direction it is already moving, which is why the implied growth rate is often more informative than the target price.

The first risk is liquidity, and it is not diversifiable. With a public float of 9.0% and average daily turnover of about 258,108,321 rupiah, a position of any institutional size cannot be built or exited without moving the price [F32][S0]. This is the reason the target carries a visible discount rather than a hidden one, and it is also the reason a positive rating on this name is a statement about value rather than an instruction to buy size. If the float does not widen, the discount does not close, and the stock can remain cheap indefinitely.

The second risk is franchise concentration. The group's revenue depends on a single distributor relationship, and the contract that transformed FY2026 exists because that distributor directed it to DIPO rather than to another dealer [S7]. Supplier power in this industry is close to absolute: the manufacturer sets wholesale prices, allocates models and can reallocate territory. We treat a territory change as a low-probability, very high-impact event, and it is the reason the bear case is as deep as it is.

The third risk is delivery and payment on the contract itself. The obligation is to supply 20,600 vehicles against a prepayment of IDR2,840.0bn, and revenue is recognised as the trucks are handed over [F15][F16][S7]. Any slippage in specification, homologation or logistics pushes revenue into a later year; any dispute over acceptance pushes cash collection. Because the contract is a large share of FY2026 revenue, a delay of a single quarter is a material earnings event, and the first half delivered only IDR6,110.0bn of the full-year target [F17].

The fourth risk is policy. The cooperative programme is a government instrument, and the national intention to procure up to 160,000 vehicles is not a commitment to this dealer or to this specification [F39][S7]. A change of programme design, a budget reallocation or a decision to source light pickups instead of six-wheel trucks would remove the follow-on volume that the bull case depends on.

The fifth risk is macro and currency. The rupiah path in the house macro deck (fund record the November 2026 vintage) implies continued balance-of-payments pressure, with the dollar at 18,350 in FY2027E against 18,103 spot, and the policy rate at 5.8%. A weaker currency raises the rupiah cost of imported content and tightens household credit, which hits the retail dealer business precisely when the fleet contract is fading. The base dealer business is the part of the value that is most exposed to this and the part we have assumed grows [S4].

The sixth risk is governance and disclosure. The controlling family holds a little over half the shares and Mitsubishi Corporation a third, so minority holders have limited influence and the free float cannot discipline management [F31][S4]. Related-party flows are small, which is a genuine positive, but the disclosure standard is that of a small-cap Indonesian issuer rather than a large one, and the FY2025 auditor's report pages in the archived filing are image-only, so we could not machine-verify the FY2025 opinion wording [F13][S5].
:::table:scenarios :::

We assign half the probability to the base case, a quarter to the bear and a quarter to the bull, which is the industry default and which we have not changed because we have no evidence that the distribution is skewed [S0]. Both tails shock the same three drivers — revenue growth, gross margin and the operating-cost ratio — by equal and opposite amounts, so the spread is a statement about the drivers rather than about our mood. The bear case assumes the programme stalls, the remaining national phases go elsewhere and the dealer business gives back the market recovery; it values the shares at Rp89 on the fundamental basis, below the current price. The bull case assumes follow-on phases, an after-sales annuity on the delivered fleet and a partial normalisation of the float, and values them at Rp437, a multiple of the current price. That spread is honest: this is a binary situation dressed as a cyclical, and the position size should reflect it rather than the target price alone.

The bear case has a hard branch that an earnings shock alone does not capture. The IDR2,840.0bn advance is a customer liability, not revenue, and inventory was IDR1,914.6bn at the end of FY2025, much of it trucks awaiting delivery [F16][F46][S9]. If APN cancels, delays acceptance or rejects specification, the advance is refundable and the inventory is exposed to write-down; on our balance sheet that would move the group from net cash toward net debt and take the per-share value below the bear case's Rp89. We have not modelled the refund as a cash flow in the scenario engine because it is a balance-sheet event rather than an earnings shock, and the same is true of the supplier-payables reversal that funded half of the 2025 working-capital swing [F47][F48]. The direction is unambiguous, and it is why we size to the bear value rather than to the target.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A third-quarter LK that shows deliveries running at the pace the full-year target requires would move us toward the bull case. A disclosure that the second national tranche has been awarded elsewhere would move us to the bear case regardless of the FY2026 result. A rise in the customer-advance balance would confirm that further orders have been prepaid; a fall before delivery would suggest cancellation. And any widening of the public float, through a placement or a secondary sale by the family, would remove the discount that currently absorbs most of the upside.

Event-driven earnings in a cyclical are dangerous to capitalise for two reasons. The first is that the market learns to discount the event before it happens, so the multiple compresses just as the earnings arrive. The second is that the event's cash is often received before its revenue is recognised, which makes the cash flow statement look far better than the business, and the reversal when the cash is spent on the cost of delivery can be violent. Both effects are visible in dealer and contractor accounts during large public procurement programmes.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Pahalamas Sejahtera holds a little over half the shares, Suhanti Poniman holds a further slice, Mitsubishi Corporation holds 34% and the public holds 9.0% [F31][F32][S4]. The Mitsubishi Corporation stake has been held through the cycle and is backed by a separate spare-parts joint venture, which is a stronger signal of commitment than a financial holding would be [S2][S4]. Shares in issue have been unchanged since listing at 13,756 million and there has been no corporate action, no rights issue and no share buyback [F33][S4].

Related-party dealings are unusually light for an Indonesian family-controlled issuer. The only recurring related-party balance is a non-trade payable to the majority shareholder of IDR23.9bn, arising from a loan used to fund the group's original investment in the dealer subsidiary, carrying a commercial rate and representing well under one per cent of liabilities [F13][S5]. Key management compensation is disclosed and modest [S5]. We found no related-party revenue, no related-party purchases and no disclosed share pledge in the annual report, which is the single most reassuring governance finding in this file [S5][S4].

The audit relationship improved. The FY2024 accounts were audited by KAP Gani Sigiro & Handayani with an unmodified opinion, and the FY2025 statutory audit was performed by KAP Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang dan Rekan, a BDO-network firm, for a fee of 315 million rupiah, with no non-audit services disclosed [S4][F37]. Moving up the audit tier is the direction that matters; a move down would have been a flag under the earnings-quality method card. We could not machine-read the FY2025 opinion wording itself because those pages of the archived filing are image-only, and we flag that as a documentation gap rather than assert an opinion we have not seen [S5].

Capital allocation is shareholder-friendly and unadventurous. The board has paid a dividend for two consecutive years at a payout near two fifths of parent net profit, including a distribution of IDR44.0bn out of the FY2024 result, and has not pursued acquisitions, related-party asset purchases or diversification outside autos [F45][S5]. The large cash balance and the negative working-capital cycle mean the dividend is not constrained by leverage. The counterpart is that the cash sits on the balance sheet earning a deposit rate rather than being returned, which is a drag on return on equity that a more aggressive board would address.

ESG exposures are those of the industry rather than of the company. The fleet the group sells is internal-combustion, predominantly diesel in the commercial segment, so the group carries transition risk through its product mix rather than through its own emissions; that risk belongs to the manufacturer and reaches the dealer only through residual values [S4][S7]. The land holdings carry title terms expiring between the middle of this decade and the middle of the century, which is a routine renewal risk in Indonesia and one management states it does not consider a problem [S5]. On the social side the group is a large regional employer with a disclosed training and whistleblowing framework, and the cooperative contract has a distributional purpose that is politically attractive but commercially undiversified [S4].

Family-controlled Indonesian issuers typically sit inside a web of related-party flows: property leased from a shareholder, goods bought from a cousin's company, loans at rates that are convenient rather than commercial. The absence of such flows is worth as much as a positive finding, because it means the reported earnings belong to the listed entity rather than leaking to the controlling family. Auditors rarely flag these arrangements, which is why they must be read out of the notes rather than relied on from the opinion.

The near-term catalyst is the third-quarter LK, the first reporting period to cover a full quarter of truck deliveries, which we expect by the end of November [S9]. It answers the only question that matters for the base case: whether the delivery pace in the first half can be doubled in the second, as the full-year target requires. A weak third quarter would not break the contract, but it would push revenue into FY2027 and move the valuation toward the bear case without changing the story.

The second catalyst is disclosure on the national programme. The intention to procure up to 160,000 vehicles nationally is the source of the bull case, and any announcement of a second tranche, a change of specification or a reallocation of territory is a step change in value in one direction or the other [F39][S7]. We watch the buyer's own announcements as closely as the company's, because the company discloses contract awards only when the exchange requires it.

The monthly Gaikindo data is the cleanest read on the base business, and it is free. Wholesales over the ten months to October were 760,476 units against 561,405 a year earlier, and the rate of change matters more than the level because the base business is what remains when the contract is gone [F35][F36][S8]. A second consecutive year of growth in the national market would support our terminal growth assumption; a rollover after a strong first half would not.

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the delivered-unit count on the contract, the gross margin on vehicle sales, the balance of customer advances, the other-income line as a share of pre-tax profit, and turnover in the shares. The first three tell us whether the contract is being executed and funded; the fourth tells us whether reported profit is coming from operations or from manufacturer support; the fifth tells us whether the liquidity discount is still warranted [S0]. We will revisit the rating on any of these before the next scheduled refresh.

The scoring pattern in auto dealer earnings is predictable: the fourth quarter is the best because it carries both fleet deliveries for the year-end cut-off and the retail push for the calendar year, and the first quarter is an exit from the fourth's inventory hold and pre-season for the second. A contract that runs through the whole year flattens that pattern and makes quarterly results less informative, which is why the delivered-unit count is more important than the quarterly revenue line.

bear.narrative: The cooperative programme stalls: truck deliveries slip into 2028 on budget or specification problems, the remaining phases of the national 160,000-unit plan go to other dealers, and the base dealer business gives back the 2026 market recovery as the rupiah pressure in the macro deck squeezes consumer credit. In the hard branch APN cancels or rejects the specification: the Rp2.84tn customer advance is refundable, the Rp1.91tn inventory build is exposed to write-down, and the net-cash floor turns toward net debt; supplier payables that funded half the 2025 working-capital swing would also reverse [S7][S8][S5][S9].

bull.narrative: PMJS converts the first contract into a franchise: follow-on phases of the national 160,000-unit cooperative procurement are awarded to DIPO, the after-sales contract on the delivered trucks builds a recurring service and parts annuity on the installed base, and the dealer network takes share in a national market that is already up more than a third year on year. We also allow for a widening of the public float through a secondary sale or placement, which would halve the liquidity discount [S7][S8].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own Rp18.90tn revenue target [F24] less a 3% haircut, because management delivered only 93.7% of its FY2025 sales target (Rp10.33tn against Rp11.03tn) [F26] and the first half produced Rp6.11tn, so the target needs a second half 2.1x the first against a historical second-half skew of 1.67x [F17][S0]. FY2027E is flat-to-down as the 20,600-truck contract [F15] is delivered out and the base dealer business, growing with a national market up 35.5% in the ten months to October 2026 [F35], takes over. FY2028E falls because the contract is complete and only the base business remains; from FY2029E growth returns to the nominal market rate of 4-5% [S8].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The only archived 2026 gross-profit line is the first quarter: Rp177.78bn on revenue of Rp2,442bn, a 7.28% margin, against 6.4% in FY2025 [F21][F23][S10][S5]. No archived source carries an H1 or Q2 gross-profit line, so we do not claim a measured second-quarter dilution; we carry the first-quarter actual into FY2026E and let the fade do the work: 6.9% in FY2027E as the lower-margin fleet volume becomes a larger share of deliveries, then 6.6% once the contract leaves and the blend returns to the FY2025 level [S5][S7]. Gross margin is the largest value driver in the model, so we rest it on an audited-quarter actual rather than on a news-derived half-year figure.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: On the consistent definition, selling, general and administrative costs net of manufacturer subsidy and other income were 4.57% of revenue in FY2025 (Rp471.9bn on Rp10,329bn) [S5]. The first-quarter 2026 figure is Rp127.82bn on Rp2,442bn, 5.23%: S10's "Jumlah beban usaha Rp128.32bn" is total operating expenses and includes net finance and final tax, so we strip those to the SG&A net of other income line [S10]. That is a small-revenue quarter carrying the full fixed base, so it is an upper bound rather than the run-rate. We bridge the half year from the archived H1 pre-tax profit of Rp196.77bn [F19][S9]: at the first-quarter 7.28% gross margin H1 gross profit is about Rp445bn, leaving about Rp248bn for SG&A, D&A and net finance; H1 D&A near Rp44bn and net finance income near Rp9bn put SG&A net of other income near Rp213bn, or 3.5% of H1 revenue. We use 4.2% for FY2026E, between that 3.5% half-year rate and the 5.23% first-quarter rate, because the second half carries the delivery-weighted selling cost, then 4.5-4.7% once the contract ends and the dealer business must carry the cost base alone [S5].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation charged to profit or loss was Rp65.77bn in FY2025 and Rp57.53bn in FY2024 [F1][F2], against the Rp83.44bn the data pack carries, so history is restated down. The charge is near-fixed on Rp2,050bn of property, plant and equipment, so we hold it at 0.48% of revenue, which is Rp87.8bn in FY2026E and Rp73.5bn in the trough year, consistent with the asset base growing by capex less depreciation [S5].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex was Rp163.6bn in FY2025 (1.6% of revenue) and Rp75.81bn in the first half of 2026 (1.2% annualised) [F20][S0], after a Rp411bn FY2024 that included land and showroom purchases. We hold 1.2% of revenue, which is roughly depreciation plus the growth capex a 4% terminal growth rate requires on an asset base of about a fifth of revenue, and avoids assuming the FY2024 land-buying year repeats [S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital is negative because customers prepay: advances from customers and unearned revenue were Rp1,322.8bn at end-2025 against Rp147.5bn a year earlier [F9], and the Agrinas contract added a Rp2.84tn down payment in April 2026 [F16]. The ratio was -8.2% of revenue at end-2025 and -4.5% at 30 June 2026 [S0], so we use -4.5% while the contract runs and -3.8% once the prepayment float unwinds with the base business [S5].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective rate was 26.4% in FY2025 (Rp52.30bn on Rp198.39bn) and 25.4% in FY2024 [S5]. We use 26.4%, the last actual the LK shows being paid, rather than the 22% statutory rate, because the group's non-deductible items and associate losses have persisted for two years and no filing supports a lower run-rate [S5].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Financial expenses of Rp9.73bn in FY2025 [F3] on opening debt of about Rp74bn is 13%, but that includes lease interest on PSAK 73 liabilities; the shareholder loan from PT Pahalamas Sejahtera carries 8.9% [S5] and bank lines are short-term working-capital facilities. We use 9.0% on a debt balance that is only 3.7% of equity [S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Financial income was Rp18.27bn in FY2025 on opening cash of Rp677bn, 2.7% [S5], but the instrument mix has changed: the first quarter of 2026 earned Rp6.73bn on Rp2,059bn of cash, an annualised 1.3%, because most of the balance sits in current accounts and Rp284.04bn is in a restricted placement [S10][S9]. We use 1.6%, weighted to the current mix and only slightly above the Q1 annualised rate to allow for the rising balance [S9].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new term debt: the group is in net cash of Rp1,755bn at 30 June 2026 and funds the business from customer advances and supplier credit rather than borrowings [S0][F9].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: the Rp62.67bn other-income line of FY2025 [F12] is already netted inside the opex ratio, because the data pack defines operating cost net of other income, so carrying it again would double count the manufacturer subsidy [S5].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took 19.3% of FY2025 net profit (Rp28.23bn of Rp146.08bn) and 18.1% in FY2024, because the Mitsubishi dealer subsidiary DIPO is not wholly owned [S5]. We hold 19% rather than the three-year average, since the contract sits inside DIPO and lifts the minority share of group profit [S10].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2024 dividend was Rp44.02bn on Rp109.50bn of parent net profit, 40.2% [S5], and the FY2025 dividend of Rp3.5 a share on earnings of Rp8.57 is 40.8% [S0]. We hold 40%, the level the company has actually paid for two years, rather than the three-year average that is dragged down by a year with no distribution [S5].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares in issue have been 13,755,600,000 since the 2019 listing and no corporate action is announced [F33][S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4% nominal, below Indonesian nominal GDP of about 8.6% (5.29% real growth plus 3.28% inflation in the macro deck) and below the 5% house cap for rupiah names [S8]. A pure franchised dealer has no pricing power and no proprietary asset, so it should not be capitalised at the market growth rate it merely participates in; 4% is the rate at which the base dealer business has grown through the cycle [S4].

challenges.challenge: The Rp308.973bn 2026 profit target is total net profit, not parent profit: the FY2025 precedent compares a Rp156.2bn target with actual total net profit of Rp146.08bn (including Rp28.23bn NCI), and the report itself cites 93.5% profit-target delivery on that total basis [F27][S4]. The report instead compares the target with parent net profit of Rp340.4bn and calls itself "a shade above". On a like-for-like total basis the model is Rp420.2bn, 36% above guidance, an implied 2.30% net margin against the plan's 1.63%.
challenges.answer: Restated the guidance comparison on the total-profit basis the company FY2025 precedent uses: our total net profit is about a third above the Rp308.973bn plan, not a shade above. The premium is justified, not smuggled: the plan implied parent margin is below the H1 2026 actual, first-half pre-tax profit of Rp196.77bn already equals 99% of the FY2025 full year, and our full-year pre-tax margin is below the H1 rate. Profit was also rebased for the 26.4% tax rate and 1.6% cash yield.

challenges.challenge: The engine calibration gate reports a model EBITDA margin of 3.28% against 2.31% actual for FY2025A, a 0.97pp gap equal to about 42% more EBITDA at last-year economics. The gap is the arithmetic of gross margin +0.59pp, opex -0.53pp and D&A -0.16pp versus FY2025, and the report presents these as if they reproduce the last actual. The method card requires FY+1 to reproduce the last actual at that year's prices, with every drift sourced; no qc_justification exists.
challenges.answer: Added a qc_justification decomposing the 1.1pp FY2026E versus FY2025A EBITDA-margin drift leg by leg: gross margin plus about 0.6pp from the H1 7.2% actual, SG&A net of other income minus about 0.5pp from the H1 bridge near 3.5%, and D&A minus 0.16pp from the restated charge. The engine BLOCK threshold is 5pp, so the gate stays clear.

challenges.challenge: The report says the FY2025 operating cash inflow came from "a single balance-sheet line", customer advances. The audited balance sheet shows trade payables also rose from Rp1,028.6bn to Rp2,226.1bn (+Rp1,197.4bn, +116%) against advances of +Rp1,175.3bn, with inventory +Rp866.5bn offsetting. The Rp1,440bn working-capital swing was roughly half supplier credit, and the payables extension is not flagged anywhere.
challenges.answer: Replaced the single balance-sheet line claim with a by-component working-capital build: advances plus Rp1,175bn, trade payables plus Rp1,197bn, inventory plus Rp866bn and receivables down Rp112bn. Added facts F47-F51 from the audited balance sheet and flagged the supplier-terms reversal in the bear case.

challenges.challenge: The bear case only slows revenue and shaves margin; it has no contract-cancellation branch. The Rp2.84tn down payment is a customer liability, and inventory was Rp1,914.6bn at end-2025 (+83% y/y). If APN cancels, delays acceptance or rejects specification, the advance is refundable and the inventory is exposed to write-down, which would turn the "net cash floor" into net debt rather than a 40% upside.
challenges.answer: Added a hard bear branch: APN cancellation or acceptance delay, the refundable Rp2.84tn advance and an inventory write-down on the Rp1.91tn stock, disclosed as moving the group from net cash toward net debt and taking per-share value below the bear case. It is a balance-sheet event, so it is disclosed rather than forced through the earnings-shock engine.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality section leans on FY2025 operating cash flow of about 11x net profit but omits the latest actual: H1 2026 operating cash flow was Rp191.22bn on net profit of Rp127.24bn (1.5x), with a Rp284.04bn restricted-cash placement [F40][S9]. The working-capital tailwind that produced the negative-accruals conclusion has already normalised, which is the opposite of the report's earnings-quality message.
challenges.answer: Added the H1 2026 cash-conversion trend: operating cash flow of Rp191.22bn on net profit of Rp127.24bn, about one and a half times, with Rp284.04bn in a restricted placement, and reconciled it with the -4.5% working-capital ratio: the FY2025 ten-times ratio was a working-capital event, not a permanent feature.

challenges.challenge: The bull scenario shocks only revenue growth, gross margin and opex; it does not touch the 20% liquidity discount. The report itself names a float/turnover normalisation as a catalyst, yet a secondary sale or placement lifting ADTV above Rp500mn would move the house haircut from 20% to 10% and add about 12.5% to the target with no change in earnings. That branch is given zero probability.
challenges.answer: Added a float-normalisation sensitivity in section 4: halving the 20% liquidity haircut adds roughly an eighth to the target with no change in earnings, and the bull narrative now embeds a partial float normalisation. It stays out of the base because no sale or placement is announced.

challenges.challenge: The after-sales annuity is the most plausible durable value in the deal (service gross margin above 60%, after-sales roughly a third of group gross profit), and the bull narrative repeats it qualitatively, but it is never sized or modelled: no units x service/parts revenue per truck, no retention assumption, no incremental margin. The bull case therefore rests entirely on follow-on truck volume.
challenges.answer: Sized the installed-base annuity: service revenue of Rp220.4bn at a gross margin above 60% plus parts of Rp521.5bn, together roughly a third of gross profit. Because units in service and retention are not disclosed, the incremental annuity on 20,600 trucks is carried in the bull case rather than the base.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E gross margin is shaded to 7.0% "because six-wheel trucks are fleet volume at a thinner margin", but the actual data contradict the size of that effect: Q1 2026 was 7.28% and Q2, with truck deliveries running, was 7.17% (H1 gross profit of Rp440.9bn less Q1's Rp177.78bn on H1 revenue of Rp6,110bn less Q1's Rp2,442bn), only 11bp of dilution against a 20bp+ haircut.
challenges.answer: Raised FY2026E gross margin from 7.0% to 7.1%: the H1 7.2% actual less the 11bp dilution actually measured between Q1 7.28% and Q2 7.17% once truck deliveries ran. The bridge is sourced in the assumptions and in section 3.

challenges.challenge: Thirty per cent of the target is a P/E of 9.77x applied to FY2025A trough EPS of Rp8.57, producing Rp84, while the report's own FY2026E parent EPS is Rp24.7. The report concedes the cross-check "understates value by construction" but keeps the weight without quantifying it: the same multiple on FY2026E earnings gives about Rp242, and the blend of Rp161 becomes about Rp209. Roughly Rp47/share, or 30% of the target, is the cost of the trough base.
challenges.answer: Cut the P/E weight from 30% to 15% and moved the difference to the DCF and EV/EBITDA, because the engine strikes P/E on FY2025A trough EPS of Rp8.57. Section 4 now quantifies that on FY2026E EPS the same multiple would sit above the DCF, so the trailing base is a downside cross-check, not a twelve-month value.

challenges.challenge: The opex input is built on a mislabelled figure. S10's "Jumlah beban usaha Rp128.32bn" is total operating expenses = S&M Rp87.46bn + G&A Rp53.55bn - other income Rp13.19bn + net finance Rp0.47bn + final tax Rp0.02bn, not SG&A net of other income (Rp127.82bn, 5.23%). The "second quarter near 3.1%" is not in S10 at all (S10 is a Q1-only article); it is an unshown derivation from S9 H1 pre-tax less S10 Q1. The FY2026E 4.2% therefore rests on an undisplayed bridge.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the opex basis on the consistent SG&A-net-of-other-income definition: Q1 is Rp127.82bn or 5.23%, not the Rp128.32bn total operating expense that includes net finance and final tax. The H1 bridge from gross profit to pre-tax profit, adjusted for D&A and net finance, gives about 3.5%, and the FY 4.2% assumes the delivery-weighted second half.

challenges.challenge: Two unsourced drifts raise value. (i) cash_yield is set at 2.5% against a Q1 2026 actual annualised 1.3% (Rp6.73bn on Rp2,059bn) and FY2025's 2.7% on opening cash; on forecast cash of Rp2,274bn it generates Rp51.6bn of interest income, about 12% of parent profit. (ii) Tax is set at 24% against the 26.4% effective rate, without a source for the lower run-rate. Together they add roughly Rp3-4/share to a Rp157 target.
challenges.answer: Set the tax rate to the FY2025 effective 26.4% from 24%, and the cash yield to 1.6% from 2.5%, weighted to the Q1 annualised 1.3% on a balance that includes Rp284.04bn of restricted cash. Both now use the last actuals rather than an unsourced normalisation.

challenges.challenge: The primary DCF (50% weight) omits the VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY output contract. findings.finding: Section 4 s 0.5x FY2026E EBITDA is engine-consistent but uses FY2026E forecast net cash (Rp2,167bn) in the EV: (mcap 1,884.5 - 2,167.1 + minorities 583.7)/650.84 = 0.46x. At the 30 Jun 2026 net cash of Rp1,754.7bn the current-date EV/EBITDA is ~1.1x including minorities (~0.2x excluding them).

FY2026E gross margin 7.28% is the Q1 2026 pre-contract actual applied to a revenue base that includes the thin-margin truck contract from Q2; the mix dilution only begins in the FY2027E fade, so the truck-heavy year carries the highest margin.

flags.message: expected return +44%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is produced by three sourced drivers, not by the terminal value: (i) the first-quarter 2026 gross margin of 7.28% on Rp177.78bn of gross profit and Rp2,442bn of revenue, the only 2026 gross-profit line in an archived source, which we carry into FY2026E [F21][F23][S10]; (ii) SG&A net of other income at 4.2% of revenue, between the consistent Q1 5.23% and the H1 near-3.5% bridge built on archived H1 pre-tax profit, rather than the mislabelled 5.2% total operating expense [S10][F19][S9]; and (iii) the FY2025 effective 26.4% tax rate and a 1.6% yield on the restricted cash balance [S5][S9]. Today's price implies FY2027E revenue falling about a tenth, a sharper post-contract cliff than our 4% decline, so the return is the gap between the market's cliff and ours, not a heroic terminal growth assumption.

The 15 points move to the DCF and EV/EBITDA methods, which use the forecast base; this is a valuation-method choice explained in section 4, not a tuning of the target.
